subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: asking a trusted elder for help in confessing [Action]
passage: I am Nazia, and I was on the stairs of our building when I saw Bilal from the second floor sitting on a step with a folded test paper. His sister Zainab came up and sat beside him. I heard only pieces: "Papa will shout." "I will come with you. You tell it, and I will help." They went in together. Later Zainab told me over the railing that Papa, their father, had gone quiet, then asked what the plan was, and the plan was that she would go over the fractions with Bilal every evening. When Bilal came out he was pale but standing straighter. I could not tell if he was relieved or only tired.

qa.q: What was Bilal holding while he sat on the stairs?
qa.a: Bilal was holding a folded test paper.

qa.q: How might Bilal have felt on the step, according to Nazia?
qa.a: Afraid of his father's reaction, since Nazia overheard "Papa will shout" and saw him holding the paper, though Nazia can only guess.

qa.q: What could Bilal do next to follow the plan?
qa.a: Go over the fractions with Zainab each evening and show progress, because it gives their father concrete steps to see.

qa.q: How might Zainab see her brother's fear?
qa.a: As something she could ease, since she sat with him, offered to go in with him and helped make a plan.

grounding: A boy afraid of his father's anger over a low mark first tells his older sister, who goes with him and helps him plan to improve.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: asking a trusted elder for help in confessing [Action]
passage:
Monday: Raghav got his maths test back: 11 out of 30, circled in red. His parents had to sign it by Thursday. All evening he hid in his room, imagining Papa's face.
Tuesday: He couldn't hold it in any longer. He showed the paper to his older sister, Ankita. She didn't laugh. "Okay. Which questions?" Together they looked at the wrong answers: nearly all fractions. "We'll tell Papa together after dinner tomorrow," she said, "and you'll say what you'll do." He wrote a plan: fractions practice every day, and ask his teacher for extra sums.
Wednesday: After dinner Ankita sat beside him while he handed Papa the paper. Papa frowned. Raghav read out his plan, voice shaking. Papa was quiet, then said, "Good. Show me the fractions every Sunday." He signed.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel on Monday evening?
qa.a: Afraid of Papa's anger, hiding in his room.

qa.q: What else could help Raghav keep his plan going?
qa.a: Asking Ankita to check a few fraction sums with him each week before Sunday.
Ankita didn't laugh, helped spot the fractions pattern, and sat beside him while he told Papa.

grounding: Over three days, a boy afraid of his father's reaction to a low mark tells his older sister first, who helps him explain and plan.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: asking a trusted elder for help in confessing [Action]
passage: Afraid to show your report card, are you? Sit here. When I was ten, I, Thomas, failed my English exam. Thirty-two out of a hundred. My father had a temper that could rattle the windows, and I hid that report card inside my mattress for two days. Then my older sister, Gopika, found me crying on the back steps. She read the card and said, "Hiding makes it worse, little brother. Come. I'll stand with you." That night she stood beside me in the front room while I told our father, and she helped me explain: the grammar had beaten me, and she would help me every evening. His face went red, then slowly calmed. He said, "You told me yourself. Now work." And Gopika-chechi kept her word for a whole term.

qa.q: How did young Thomas feel for those two days?
qa.a: Scared, hiding the card and ending up crying on the back steps.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made the difference?
qa.a: Letting Gopika go with him and explaining with a plan for the grammar, instead of hiding the card any longer.

qa.q: How might Gopika have felt standing beside Thomas?
qa.a: Protective and caring, enough to keep helping him every evening for a whole term.

grounding: An elder recalls being afraid to show a failing mark and asking an older sister to go with him to tell their father.
